blocks.text: [II, 524] ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE PART TWO BOOK ONE ON ON THE CLEAN BIRDS. [col. 1]
On the Hebrew name of the dove.

The sacred writers touch on the clean birds only briefly, with the single exception of the dove, about which they say more than about all the others taken together. It is therefore necessary to treat it more carefully. It is held that the dove is called in Hebrew יונה jona from the verb ינה jana, which means to oppress, as if it lay open to the plundering of all. On this point the poets are cited:
Censure pardons the ravens and harasses the doves.

This seems far-fetched. I shall therefore try to offer something more probable. In Jerem. XLVI, 16. and L, 16. the Hebrew words מפני חרב היונה are rendered by the Greeks ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας Ἑλληνικῆς [apo prosōpou machairas Hellēnikēs], from the face of the Greek sword; by Jerome, from the face of the sword of the dove; by the Syriac, from the face of the sword ܡܣܝܒܐ of the tormentor; by R. Selomo and Kimchi, האונסת, of the oppressor. But the Chaldee Paraphrast has מן קדם חרב סנאה דהיא כחמר מרויא, from the face of the hostile sword, which is like intoxicating wine, as if היונה were formed from יין, that is, from wine, with Yod and Vav interchanged. From the same source, then, יונה jona for the dove could be derived. If we follow this, יונה jona will properly be the οἰνὰς [oinas], a kind of wild dove so named from wine. 1. Because, on the authority of Eustathius, it is οἰνωπὸς τὸ χρῶμα [oinōpos to chrōma], that is, because it resembles wine, or ripe grapes, in colour. 2. Because it usually appears at the time of the vintage. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3: Οἰνὰς δὲ τοῦ [col. 2] φθινοπώρου καὶ φαίνεται μάλιστα, καὶ ἁλίσκεται· [Oinas de tou phthinopōrou kai phainetai malista, kai halisketai] The oenas (or, as Gaza renders it, vinago) appears and is caught chiefly in autumn. Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11: Ἡ δὲ φὰψ, καὶ ἡ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· ἡ δὲ οἰνὰς φθινοπώρῳ μόνῳ· [Hē de phaps, kai hē peristera aei phainontai; hē de oinas phthinopōrō monō] The smaller wood pigeon and the dove are always to be seen; but the vinago only in autumn. But this etymology [II, 525] is contradicted by the usage of the Hebrews, among whom יונה jona, or יון jon, is not the οἰνὰς [oinas] but the dove in general, and properly the domestic one. Accordingly the οἰνὰς [oinas] dove was called by the Syrians ܟܪܡܝܘܢ charmion, or ܟܪܡܝܘܢܐ charmiona, a word compounded of two, ܟܪܡ and ܝܘܢ, or ܝܘܢܐ, of which the former means vine and the latter dove. This was the very name of one of those famous handmaids of Cleopatra. In Greek it is written Χάρμιον [Charmion], or Χαρμιόνη [Charmionē], or Χαρμιουνώ [Charmiounō]. Plutarch in the Antony: Εἴρας ἡ Κλεοπάτρας κουρεύτρια, καὶ Χάρμιον, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὰ μέγιστα διοικεῖται τῆς ἡγεμονίας· [Eiras hē Kleopatras koureutria, kai Charmion, hyph᾽ hōn ta megista dioikeitai tēs hēgemonias] Iras, Cleopatra's hairdresser, and Charmion, by whom the most important affairs of the realm were managed. And further on, regarding the death of Cleopatra: Τῶν δὲ γυναικῶν ἡ μὲν Εἴρας λεγομένη πρὸς τοῖς ποσὶν ἀπέθνησκεν· ἡ δὲ Χάρμιον, ἤδη σφαλλομένη, καὶ καρηβαροῦσα, κατεκόσμει τὸ διάδημα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς. [Tōn de gynaikōn hē men Eiras legomenē pros tois posin apethnēsken; hē de Charmion, ēdē sphallomenē, kai karēbarousa, katekosmei to diadēma peri tēn kephalēn autēs] Of her women, the one called Iras had died at her feet; Charmion, however, already tottering and heavy-headed, was adorning her head with the diadem. Galen, On theriac to Piso, book 1, chapter 8: Καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι λεγόμεναι Νάειρα, καὶ Καρμιόνη· ἡ μὲν ἀναπλέκουσα τὰς τρίχας εὐπρεπῶς, ἡ δὲ [col. 3] ἀποτέμνουσα τὰς ὑπεροχὰς τῶν ὀνύχων εὐφυῶς. [Kai tois onomasi legomenai Naeira, kai Karmionē; hē men anaplekousa tas trichas euprepōs, hē de apotemnousa tas hyperochas tōn onychōn euphyōs] And (Cleopatra's handmaids) called Naira and Carmione, of whom the former braided her hair becomingly, the latter skilfully trimmed the tips of her nails. Tzetzes, Chil. 6, Hist. 44:

Τῇ Κλεοπάτρᾳ τῇ σοφῇ, τῇ καὶ ὡραιοτάτῃ, Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δὲ σύμπασι ^{a)} πολλῶν ὑπερφερούσῃ, Πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν τριχῶν, καὶ τῶν ὀνύχων, ἦσαν Χαρμιουνὼ, καὶ Τάειρα τί δε δηλοῦσι τάδε; Σύρον τὸν Τζέτζην βλέπε νῦν, Ἰσμαηλίτην ἅμα, Καὶ ταῦτα διαρθροῦντα σοι ταῖς γλώσσαις ταῖς ἐκείνων. Κατὰ Ἑβραίων γλῶσσάν τε, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σύρων ἅμα, Χαρμὶ δηλοῖ τὴν ἀμπελον, Οὐνὼ περιστεράν δε, Τὴν, ἣν ^{b)} φησιν οἱ Ἕλληνες περιστερὰν οἰνάδα, Κατὰ Ἰσμαηλίτας δὲ, τοὺς Ἄγαρ γόνους λέγω, Περιστερὰν τὴν Γάειραν σημαίνουσάν μοι νόει. [Tē Kleopatra tē sophē, tē kai hōraiotatē, / Kai tois loipois de sympasi ^{a)} pollōn hyperpherousē, / Pros epimeleian trichōn, kai tōn onychōn, ēsan / Charmiounō, kai Taeira ti de dēlousi tade? / Syron ton Tzetzēn blepe nyn, Ismaēlitēn hama, / Kai tauta diarthrounta soi tais glōssais tais ekeinōn. / Kata Hebraiōn glōssan te, kai tēn tōn Syrōn hama, / Charmi dēloi tēn ampelon, Ounō peristeran de, / Tēn, hēn ^{b)} phēsin hoi Hellēnes peristeran oinada, / Kata Ismaēlitas de, tous Agar gonous legō, / Peristeran tēn Gaeiran sēmainousan moi noei.]
